data.title: Vancomycin
data.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** Glycopeptide antibiotic

## Mechanism of action
- Binds D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of cell-wall precursors → blocks peptidoglycan polymerisation → bactericidal (Gram-positives only)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Not absorbed orally (oral form only for C. difficile colitis); IV; renal excretion

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Serious MRSA infections: complicated skin and soft-tissue infection, bacteraemia, osteomyelitis
- Severe staphylococcal/streptococcal infections in β-lactam allergy
- Oral vancomycin: C. difficile colitis

## Dose & formulations
- 15–20 mg/kg IV every 8–12 h, infused slowly (at least 60 min); dosing guided by AUC/trough levels

## Adverse effects
- Vancomycin infusion reaction ('red man' / flushing syndrome): flushing, itch, hypotension of upper body from direct histamine release with fast infusion — slow the infusion, give antihistamine (not true allergy)
- Drug-induced linear IgA bullous dermatosis — vancomycin is the commonest cause
- DRESS (HLA-A*32:01), SJS/TEN
- Nephrotoxicity (especially with piperacillin–tazobactam, aminoglycosides), ototoxicity, neutropenia

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, cyclosporine: additive toxicity

## Monitoring
- Serum levels (AUC/trough), renal function, CBC on long courses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Use if needed (monitor levels).

## Viva points
- Red man syndrome = infusion-rate reaction, not allergy
- Commonest cause of drug-induced linear IgA disease
- DRESS linked to HLA-A*32:01

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 (Vancomycin); Wolverton 4e ch.9 and ch.67 (Cutaneous drug reactions). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
